resources.string: The libraries that make Storage Studio work
Storage Studio is built on open source software. We are grateful to the projects below and distribute them under their respective licenses.
Large photos open sharp and zoomable, without switching each time

Affects only what the Network tool displays — no app feature depends on it. When on, the IP of each connection is looked up to show a host name (a reverse-DNS query); those lookups are the only network traffic this app itself sends. When off, connections just show the owner (e.g. Google) and the IP, and the app sends nothing.

Stream recordings to a machine on your network running the collector script — kept in SQLite with no on-device row limit. Great for long capture runs. When on, each monitor tool can choose to also stream to it while recording.

Run ./tools/collect.sh on your computer (starts the collector; sets up USB and asks which device if several are connected), then open http://localhost:8899 for guided setup, copy-paste URLs and live results. Enter the http://<your-ip>:<port> it shows here — or, over USB, use http://127.0.0.1:8899.

Every permission carries one protection level, set by whoever defined it. This is the primary badge.

Defined by an app rather than the Android platform. This is separate from protection level — a custom permission still has one, so it also counts under Dangerous, Signature, and so on. That\'s why the category totals add up to more than the permission count.

With Shizuku or root connected you can flip a permission on or off for an app right here — tap a permission (or a matrix cell) to open its sheet and use the switch. Dangerous permissions toggle with pm; special app-op permissions (all-files access, draw over apps, install unknown apps…) toggle with appops. Signature and normal permissions are fixed at install and stay read-only.

Pick at least one provider to watch first.

Content providers are Android\'s shared data stores — media, contacts, SMS, call log, calendar, settings and every app\'s own. This tool registers change observers on the ones you pick and logs each change, so you can see the device\'s data mutations as they happen — the complement to App-ops, which shows access rather than change.
On Android 11+ each change reports whether it was an insert, update or delete. Older releases only say a change happened (shown as \"change\").
SMS, contacts, call log and calendar only deliver changes to apps holding their read permission. Shell access is available, so those are granted to this app automatically when you enable them.
SMS, contacts, call log and calendar only deliver changes to apps holding their read permission. Without shell access those providers may stay silent; media and settings work regardless.
Copy something and it appears here. Android only exposes the clipboard while this app is in front.
Android 10+ only lets the foreground app read the clipboard, so clips are captured while this screen is open — and kept across restarts.

Android 10+ only exposes the clipboard to the app that\'s in the foreground (or the active keyboard). This tool can only capture clips while its screen is open — there\'s no way to monitor the clipboard in the background without being a keyboard or having system access. What it captures is kept on device across restarts.

Android apps ship as portable bytecode. ART can compile it ahead-of-time to native machine code for faster startup and execution, at the cost of disk space. Pick how much to compile below — the current state and footprint update after each run.

This app is debuggable, so Android keeps it at “verify” and won\'t ahead-of-time compile it — these actions won\'t change the state or size. Try a normal (release) app to see them take effect.

Compile every method to native. Fastest startup and runtime, larger on disk.
Compile all code, even rarely used. Maximum optimization, biggest footprint.
No native compilation — interpret + JIT. Smallest on disk; slower first runs.
